extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, psychologists, students and researchers of humor theory and rhetorical technique
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and categorizing techniques/strategies Freud identifies as constitutive of wit (rhetorical, psychological, logical mechanisms such as sophisms, unification, allusion, representation through opposites, omission, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of "faulty thinking" (sophism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique of wit that consists of establishing 'faulty thinking'—a semblance of logic or sophistical reasoning that conceals erroneous combination or neglect (e.g., treating separate faults individually and refusing to combine them into a sum-total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud illustrates with marriage-agent stories and the kettle example: each separate protest or evasion is plausible alone but together they contradict or ignore cumulative depreciation. The witty effect arises from the appearance of logical reasoning (sophism) that actually misleads. Anti-pattern: presenting truly coherent, cumulative reasoning will not produce this effect. Scoring notes: look for surface logical form that conceals inconsistency (e.g., using 'and' where 'either–or' is required, isolating factors that should be summed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic errors of thought (automatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated, habitual modes of response that continue inappropriately into contexts where they become the opposite of the speaker's intention; the automatism of habit produces self-betrayal and comic exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the agent's assistant who mindlessly echoes praise and thus amplifies a conceded flaw; a marriage agent who, carried away, lists further faults. The technique is effective when repetition/echo becomes maladaptive. Practical note: contrast intended persuasive speech with automatic repetition that undoes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming an unexpected identity or surprising correlation between two related but distinct relationships/terms so that they unify into a single wittily framed idea (analogous to condensation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lichtenberg's January/good-wishes joke; the division of life into two complementary halves; repartee as turning the defender's words into an attack ('paying with the same coin'). Unification often creates witty repartee by establishing identity between attack and counterattack. Look for surprising analogies, mirrors, or mappings that bind two separate relations into one striking formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting the opposite (or a 'yes...but' that functions as 'no') for the only logically proper answer, producing wit by deliberate inversion; this technique underlies irony as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's clergyman/ghosts example ('Yes, at your pleasure, but they won't come') shows how 'yes...but' serves as equivalent to 'no'. Representation through the opposite can produce irony (Marc Antony's 'For Brutus was an honorable man' is given as parallel). Note: technique alone does not define wit—contextual purpose matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outdoing-wit (exaggerated opposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An intensified form of representation-through-opposite where the speaker goes beyond the natural opposite to an even stronger, exaggerated formulation that dramatizes the hidden thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the surgeon who, after royal applause, asks if the king desires amputation of the other leg; Lessing's epigram about dyed hair. This technique exaggerates the implied meaning to greater effect. Look for replies that amplify the implicit criticism or assertion to an absurd or hyperbolic degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect expression (representation through relationships and associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying something by implication via associative chains or relational parallels rather than stating it directly; Freud groups unification, representation through the opposite, and other techniques under 'indirect expression.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the American anecdote where two portraits prompt 'And where is the Savior?'—the critic implies 'you are thieves' by allusion to Christ between thieves. The mechanism: evoke a familiar triadic/relational image and omit the central element to imply condemnation. Effective allusion requires shared cultural knowledge; weak or opaque associations reduce wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion (indirect expression with substitution or similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a familiar phrase, structure, or sound to evoke another idea indirectly—similar sentence structures, puns, or modified quotations suggest an unspoken target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'New baths heal well' alluding to 'New brooms clean well'; 'The trip around the Wilt (world)' punning on Verne. Subtypes include sound/sentence-similarity, small modifications, and condensed substitutions. Guidance: successful allusion hinges on audience recognition of the source; the less explicit the substitution, the more 'witty' (but also more fragile) the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission as allusion (omission without substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving out a linking or explanatory element so that the audience fills the gap by inference; the omission functions as an allusive gap that carries the witticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: remarks like 'When X. hears this he will receive another box on his ear' omit the causal chain (he'll write an article prompting assault); Heine's line about pastils. The wit depends on the audience completing the unstated inference. Caution: omission must still leave a reasonable inferential path; too obscure an omission fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination / addition of 'and' (witty enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating wit by coordinating heterogeneous items (especially inserting a surprising or incongruous item via 'and') so that the conjunction signals an unexpected link or equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heine's listing 'students, professors, Philistines, and cattle' uses 'and' to indicate a pointed correlation; 'with a fork and with much effort his mother pulled him from a mess' misattributes 'effort' as an instrument. Use this when juxtaposing items so that the middle placement or conjunction reframes meaning. Overuse reduces sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning / manifold application of the same material (condensation/pun)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a single lexical item or phrase in two senses (double meaning) or applying the same material in multiple senses (manifold application) to produce a witty identity or paradox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud contrasts this with unification; examples include puns and cases where a word's frequent/common meaning dominates while a remote meaning supplies the joke. Watch for contexts where identical wording maps to two conceptually distinct referents and produces surprise or new identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the minute or minutest element
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering the whole character or situation by focusing on an insignificant or trivial detail that evokes the larger reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud introduces this as a subgroup of indirect representation: a tiny, telling detail (the minutest element) is used to represent the entirety. Effective when the trivial detail is strongly and recognizably linked to the broader trait or circumstance. Example seeds appear at the end of the chunk; look for jokes that spotlight a small physical or behavioral sign that stands in for the whole.
